# Version Control with Git and GitHub for Automation Projects

## Overview
As you start writing scripts and building serious workflows, you need a way to track changes, undo mistakes, back up your work, and collaborate - and Git with GitHub is the universal industry standard for exactly that, so learning it is non-negotiable for a professional. Git is a version-control system that records snapshots of your project over time. Each meaningful change is saved as a commit with a message describing it, so you build a full history you can review and, if something breaks, roll back to a working version - a lifesaver when an automation script suddenly stops working. The core everyday commands are few: git init starts tracking a project, git add stages the files you changed, git commit saves them with a message, and git log shows the history. Branches let you work on a new feature or experiment in isolation without touching the working version, then merge it back when it is ready - essential for safe changes and teamwork. GitHub is the most popular place to host your Git repositories online: you push your commits there to back them up and share them, and pull requests let others review changes before they are merged, which is how teams collaborate. For automation specifically, Git is where you store your Python scripts and, importantly, exported workflow definitions - n8n workflows and Make/Zapier blueprints can be exported as JSON and version-controlled, so you track how your automations evolve. A critical safety habit is using a .gitignore file to keep secrets (API keys, .env files) out of the repository, since committing credentials to GitHub is a common and dangerous mistake. Beyond the practical benefits, a well-organized GitHub profile becomes part of your portfolio, showing employers real, documented work.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: Why version control matters for automation; Git basics: init, add, commit, log; Branches and merging; Pushing to GitHub and pull requests; Storing exported workflows and .gitignore for secrets. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Create a GitHub repository for your automation work, initialize Git locally, commit your Day 21 script, add a .gitignore that excludes .env, create a branch to make a change, and merge it back.
Mini Project: Set up a well-structured automation project repo on GitHub containing your scripts and at least one exported workflow (n8n/Make JSON), with a clear README, a .gitignore for secrets, and a history of meaningful commits.
Assignment: Explain what a commit, a branch, and a pull request are in your own words, and describe why committing an API key to GitHub is dangerous and how .gitignore prevents it.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
